questions.question: How are strings compared in Go?
questions.title: String equality and ordering
questions.direct_answer: Go strings are comparable with `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, and `>=`. Equality requires identical byte sequences, and ordering is lexicographic by byte values. The comparison is case-sensitive, does not normalize Unicode, and does not apply locale-aware collation, so visually similar or canonically equivalent text can compare unequal.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether exact representation comparison is separated from normalization, folding, and collation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming string ordering is locale-aware or that visually equal Unicode text always has equal bytes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete identity design that stores a canonical key separately from display text.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: String equality compares the complete byte sequences.
Unicode normalization is not performed automatically.
Locale-aware user sorting requires a collation solution beyond operators.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Go string operators compare the bytes stored in the values. Two strings are equal only when they have the same length and identical bytes. Ordering compares bytes lexicographically, so it gives a stable language-defined order suitable for keys and deterministic technical sorting. It is not a natural-language dictionary order.

Case remains significant: `"Go" != "go"`. Unicode normalization is also not automatic. A precomposed `é` and an `e` followed by a combining accent may render alike but have different byte sequences and therefore compare unequal. The language does not know whether an application wants normalization, case folding, or locale-specific collation.

For example, a map keyed by usernames treats different byte spellings as different keys. If the product requires case-insensitive normalized identities, it should compute and store a documented canonical key while retaining the display spelling separately. Applying only `strings.ToLower` is not a complete answer for every script or locale.

Direct comparison is ideal for protocol tokens, identifiers with an exact encoding contract, hashes represented in one canonical form, and ordinary exact values. For human-facing search and sorting, I define normalization, folding, and collation requirements explicitly and use appropriate Unicode tooling before comparing.

sections.title: Operators compare representation, not linguistic meaning
sections.content:
Byte-wise comparison is simple, deterministic, and consistent with string map keys. It avoids hidden locale state and gives every program the same result for the same bytes. That predictability is valuable for protocols and storage.

Human text equivalence is contextual. Normalization can align canonically equivalent sequences; case folding can align selected case variants; collation can order words for a locale. These are transformations or algorithms layered above the string operators.

sections.title: Exact bytes versus visual similarity
sections.content:
| Pair | Byte-equal? | Reason |
|---|---:|---|
| `"Go"`, `"Go"` | Yes | Identical bytes |
| `"Go"`, `"go"` | No | Case changes one byte |
| precomposed `é`, decomposed `e + accent` | No | Different UTF-8 sequences |
| normalized canonical keys | Depends on chosen policy | Transformation occurs before equality |

sections.title: Compare two visually similar Unicode spellings
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    precomposed := "é"
    decomposed := "e\u0301"
    fmt.Println("Go" == "go")
    fmt.Println(precomposed == decomposed)
    fmt.Printf("% x\n% x\n", []byte(precomposed), []byte(decomposed))
}
```
Both comparisons are false. The hexadecimal output shows different UTF-8 byte sequences for the two forms of `é`.

questions.question: When should you use `strings.EqualFold` for case-insensitive comparison?
questions.title: Case-insensitive comparison with EqualFold
questions.direct_answer: Use `strings.EqualFold` when two UTF-8 strings should be compared using Unicode simple case folding. It is clearer and generally more correct than lowercasing both strings merely for equality. It does not perform Unicode normalization, full multi-character folding, or locale-specific matching, so security identifiers and natural-language search still need an explicit canonicalization policy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether simple folding, allocation, normalization, locale, and persistent identity policies are distinguished.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating EqualFold as Unicode normalization or a complete canonicalization strategy for account identifiers.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why a comparison predicate is different from choosing a stored canonical key.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `EqualFold` applies Unicode simple case folding for equality.
It avoids allocating two lowercased strings just for comparison.
It handles more than ASCII case pairs.
It does not normalize canonically equivalent byte sequences.
It is not locale-aware or a complete security canonicalization rule.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`strings.EqualFold(a, b)` answers whether two UTF-8 strings are equal under Unicode simple case folding. It communicates case-insensitive intent directly and avoids creating lowercase copies only to compare them. For ordinary case-insensitive command words or labels, it is usually a better first choice than `strings.ToLower(a) == strings.ToLower(b)`.

Simple folding groups code points in case-equivalence classes, so the behaviour goes beyond ASCII. It deliberately does not implement every linguistic transformation. For example, the package documents that `EqualFold("ß", "ss")` is false because that would require full folding across a different number of code points.

For example, `EqualFold("Go", "gO")` is true, while exact equality is false. A precomposed and decomposed accented spelling remains different unless the application normalizes both first. Locale-sensitive cases, such as product-specific Turkish text handling, require a policy beyond simple folding.

I use EqualFold for comparison, not as a stored canonical key by itself. Authentication names, filesystem-like identifiers, and database uniqueness need one documented normalization and case policy applied consistently at every layer. EqualFold is a useful predicate, but it cannot replace those storage and security decisions.

sections.title: Case folding is one transformation layer
sections.content:
Lowercasing transforms each input into another string, while EqualFold evaluates case equivalence directly. The predicate is efficient and avoids exposing one lowercase result as though it were a universal canonical spelling.

Normalization and locale are independent axes. Text can differ by canonical Unicode composition even after case is ignored, and a locale can define expectations beyond Unicode simple folding. Choose each layer because the domain requires it.

sections.title: What EqualFold does and does not promise
sections.content:
| Pair or requirement | EqualFold result/support |
|---|---|
| `Go` versus `gO` | true |
| `AB` versus `ab` | true |
| `ß` versus `ss` | false; not full multi-character folding |
| Precomposed versus decomposed accent | No normalization |
| Locale-specific collation | Not provided |

questions.question: When should you use a `string` instead of `[]byte` in Go?
questions.title: Choosing string or byte slice
questions.direct_answer: Use `string` for immutable text, comparable identifiers, map keys, and APIs that should not expose mutation. Use `[]byte` for mutable buffers, binary data, streaming I/O, and protocols where exact bytes matter. Conversion is explicit and may cost allocation and copying, so keep data in its natural representation through a pipeline instead of switching repeatedly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the choice follows mutability, comparability, I/O shape, and conversion boundaries.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using string for a frequently mutated buffer or converting between string and bytes repeatedly inside a processing loop.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that UTF-8 validity is independent of both types and that slice assignment may preserve aliasing.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Strings are immutable, comparable, and valid map keys.
Byte slices are mutable and may share backing arrays.
A string can still contain arbitrary non-UTF-8 bytes.
I/O APIs commonly use byte slices to reuse caller-provided buffers.
Convert once near a representation boundary when possible.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A string communicates an immutable sequence of bytes and supports equality, ordering, and map-key use. It is the natural representation for text values, names, paths as interpreted by string APIs, and identifiers whose callers should not mutate shared contents. Valid UTF-8 is a separate contract; string itself can hold arbitrary bytes.

A byte slice communicates mutable byte-oriented storage. It is appropriate for network reads, file buffers, encoders, cryptographic inputs, compressed data, and construction that changes in place. Slices are not comparable except with nil, and assigning one slice to another can leave both views sharing the same backing array.

For example, an HTTP body arrives as bytes because I/O fills buffers and the payload might not be text. After content type and encoding are validated, application code may convert one field to string for lookup or display. Keeping the whole pipeline as repeated byte-to-string-to-byte conversions adds work and obscures ownership.

Conversion semantics prevent normal mutation of a byte slice from changing an existing string, but a runtime cost may exist. I choose the representation from mutability, operations, and boundary meaning. Text processing usually remains string-based; binary and reusable buffer processing remains byte-based until a deliberate conversion point.

sections.title: Type choice communicates ownership and permitted operations
sections.content:
String says the value cannot be edited through this reference and may participate in value comparison. Byte slice says callers can index, mutate, append, and possibly share capacity. Those promises matter more than whether the current bytes happen to spell readable text.

Conversions are bridges, not neutral casts. Keeping a stable representation through each stage reduces copying and makes ownership easier to review. Convert where the domain changes—for example, after decoding a protocol field into application text.

sections.title: Representation trade-offs
sections.content:
| Property | `string` | `[]byte` |
|---|---|---|
| Mutable through value | No | Yes |
| Comparable / map key | Yes | No |
| May contain invalid UTF-8 | Yes | Yes |
| Natural for reusable I/O buffers | No | Yes |
| Aliasing after assignment | Immutable observation | May share backing array |
| Main role | Text or immutable bytes | Binary or mutable buffer |

sections.title: Use immutable text as a key and bytes as a buffer
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    identifier := "user-42"
    owners := map[string]string{identifier: "Mina"}

    buffer := []byte("draft")
    buffer[0] = 'D'

    fmt.Println(owners[identifier])
    fmt.Println(string(buffer))
}
```
The string works directly as a map key, while the byte slice supports in-place mutation before conversion at the display boundary.
